sources.headline: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
sources.text: Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people."It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying.BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market."The market was completely destroyed. The bombing spread terror and fear among the local population," market trader Fadlallah Adam Hamouda told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily.Another trader told the BBC the attack had come as shock as UN peacekeepers have been in Abyei since 2011 - with more than 2,800 uniformed personnel currently deployed."Our area is a weapons-free zone under United Nations protection, yet it was targeted by drones," he said."The attack caused extensive material damage after the fuel market was struck, sparking a massive fire that spread to nearby homes."Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.On Monday, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town."So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

sources.headline: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan
sources.text: A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”AFP contributed to this report

sources.headline: Sudan drone strike kills around 150 in Abyei market
sources.text:
A drone strike in a busy market in the disputed region of Abyei has killed more than 150 people, according to local officials.
South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military for the attack, without providing evidence, amid the long-running civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which is reportedly active in the Abyei area.
The special UN mission in Abyei warned in May that the RSF's presence in the resource-rich region had put residents in additional danger, and risked intensifying the older territorial dispute between Sudan and the world's newest sovereign state, South Sudan.
Satellite images gave a sense of the scale of the damage after the large fire triggered by the drone strikesImage: Planet Labs PBC/REUTERS
What do we know about the drone strike?
According to local authorities, the attack hit the busy Amiet Market at around midday on Monday. Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker information minister in Abyei, told Reuters news agency on Tuesday that the death toll had more than doubled, reaching at least 153 compared to a stated figure of 73 the previous day.
He said that Sudan's military was responsible for the attack but did not provide evidence. Akol Ngor said around 8,000 people had been displaced by the bombing.
South Sudan's Foreign Ministry also blamed the Sudanese army and said the drone struck multiple locations around the busy market.
One of these, judging by witness accounts, was a fuel depot — and this led to a large fire that proved difficult to bring under control overnight and was still ablaze on Tuesday.
South Sudan said it had summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to "refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property."
Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders, said that its staff was treating some 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted," said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF's medical activities manager at the hospital.
Many of the wounded were taken to Ameth Bek hospital for treatmentImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS
What's the backstory of Sudan, South Sudan and Abyei?
The oil-rich Abyei region's status was not resolved by the 2005 peace agreement that broadly ended decades of civil war in Sudan.
It was also not settled in 2011 when South Sudan became an independent country.
A referendum was planned but never materialized, stalling over disputes on who should be allowed to vote. This left Abyei in a state of limbo, jointly administered and with an interim UN security force on site for 15 years.
The region's majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan.
Amiet Market, the site of the attack, is an important trading hub for both communities.
The unstable region has also experienced intercommunal violence in recent years between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities and is home to other armed militias.
Medecins Sans Frontieres said its staff were providing surgical services, wound dressing and other emergency care to more than 20 woundedImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS
How does this fit into Sudan's army's war with the RSF?
The April 2023 outbreak of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary — which has turned into a conflict with fairly entrenched battle lines, putting Sudan into a de facto state of partition — is increasing tension in the already-strained region.
Abyei borders South Kordofan state in Sudan, which has become a major center of fighting in the war.
Sudan's military alleges that the RSF is also operating out of Abyei. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) issued a similar statement in May.
Officials in Abyei and South Sudan dispute this, however.
Sudan's military and the RSF have both been using drones extensively in the conflict.
"We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure — these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York on Tuesday when asked about the attack.

More than 150 killed in Sudan drone strike on disputed Abyei border region
AFRICA

At least 153 people have been killed in a drone strike on a market in the disputed Abyei region, where a fire at a nearby fuel depot continued to burn on Tuesday. Local officials blamed Sudan’s military for Monday’s attack, which also left dozens injured. 

Issued on: 20/10/2026 - 18:24

2 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
File photo: Residents at the market in the town of Abyei, central Sudan, Wednesday, December 12, 2007. © Alfred de Montesquiou, AP

A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, hit a nearby fuel depot, killing at least 153 people and igniting a fire that was still burning Tuesday, a local official said.

Yohanna Akol Ngor, the Abyei administration’s caretaker information minister, blamed Sudan ’s military for Monday's attack on Amiet Market, north of Abyei town.

READ MORE
Drone attacks kill scores in Sudan's West Kordofan state and capital Khartoum

“We have recorded 153 deaths,” Akol told The Associated Press by phone Tuesday. He said the death toll continued to rise as the fire burned.

The motive for the attack was not immediately clear, and the AP could not independently verify who carried it out.

READ MORE
Sudanese slowly rebuild war-ravaged capital Khartoum

Sudan’s military did not respond to a request for comment.

Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said more than 20 wounded people were brought to Ameth Bek Hospital, where MSF teams were working alongside staff from South Sudan’s Health Ministry.

“So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted,” said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF’s medical activities manager at the hospital.

South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry also blamed Sudan’s military, saying the attack hit multiple locations within the market, causing civilian casualties and extensive property damage.

The ministry said it had summoned Sudan’s ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to “refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property”. It called for issues concerning Abyei to be addressed through diplomatic channels.

Sudan’s military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have been fighting since April 2023, devastating large parts of the country and threatening stability along its borders.

WATCH MORE
Fears for South Sudan peace after arrest of vice president

Akol said the strike hit around 11am Monday. He said the fuel depot supplied local businesses.

“It is a horrible and shocking situation,” he said.

MSF called on all parties to stop attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, expressing concern about people’s ability to safely reach healthcare and other essential services.

Amiet Market is a trading hub serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities.

The oil-rich Abyei region’s status was left unresolved by a 2005 peace agreement that ended decades of civil war and remained unsettled when South Sudan became independent in 2011. A proposed referendum stalled over disagreements about who could vote.

The region’s majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favour Sudan. Abyei has also experienced deadly communal violence, including fighting over land between Ngok Dinka and neighbouring Twic Dinka communities.

(FRANCE 24 with AP)

sources.headline: 160 reported killed in escalating drone attacks across Sudan
sources.text: Rights groups warn increasing attacks by unmanned aircraft on civilians and infrastructure.A wave of drone attacks across Sudan has killed more than 160 people in recent days, according to medics and rights groups.Drone attacks on the capital, Khartoum, killed three children on Monday, according to Emergency Lawyers, a group that monitors violence against civilians in Sudan’s civil war, while more than 160 were reported to have been killed in western regions since Friday.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Air strike in Sudan kills UN aid truck driver: WFPlist 2 of 3Conflict, drought increasing risk of famine in Sudan: Monitorlist 3 of 3Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogueend of listThe attacks were blamed on the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and government troops, who have been fighting since 2023. The increasing use of drones in recent months has caused growing numbers of civilian casualties.The deadliest recent attack was near a market on Sunday evening in al-Dabba town in the southwestern state of West Kordofan, controlled by the RSF. Residents and medical workers said a drone attacked a transport hub where villagers had gathered after a market day to find rides home, killing 80 people.Another 47 wounded people were taken to the nearby town of al-Mujlad, where 30 later died from their injuries, a medical source said, according to the AFP news agency.The RSF’s self-declared administration, known as Tasis, and Emergency Lawyers accused the army of carrying out the attack.Attacks on damsIn eastern Sudan, a military source said on Sunday that air defences intercepted several RSF drones targeting the Atbara and Setit dams in Gadarif state, about 420km east of Khartoum. There was no immediate comment from the RSF.Early on Monday, another drone attack hit the RSF stronghold of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Medical and RSF sources said 17 people, including seven RSF officers, were killed and 23 wounded.An RSF drone attack on Friday hit a gathering of displaced people in Sudan’s Blue Nile province on the border with Ethiopia, killing 41 people, Emergency Lawyers said.The group condemned the attack, calling it a humanitarian tragedy.The United Nations also condemned the deadly attacks.“We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting central services,” Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told reporters on Monday.Sudanese refugees arrive at Oure Cassoni camp in Chad to escape war in Sudan, February 24, 2026 [Dan Kitwood/Getty]At least 59,000 killedThe Sudan war began in April 2023 when military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF top commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as Hemedti, fell out over plans to fold the paramilitary into the army.In June this year, Hemedti was sentenced to death in his absence for war crimes.However, the fighting, now in its fourth year, continues and has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED. Aid groups say the actual death toll is likely higher.The UN says about 13 million people have been forced from their homes, creating what aid groups call the world’s largest humanitarian crisis.Across Sudan, 33.7 million people, including 17.3 million children, urgently need food support this year. An estimated 825,000 children face severe acute malnutrition, according to the UN.The United States on Friday urged the UN Security Council to push for a humanitarian truce and expand an arms embargo on Sudan, but China and Russia opposed widening the embargo.
